1440: They paid me three times the going rate to carry one sealed note and forget I had ever met them.
1441: They asked how fast I could run, and looked delighted the answer was faster than they had hoped.
1442: They handed me a note, wanted no reply, and paid as though a reply would only invite trouble.
1443: They pressed extra coins into my hand for each detail about them I agreed to forget.
1444: They gave me a sealed message, paid triple, and asked me to describe them as utterly unremarkable.
1445: They wanted the note carried fast and their appearance carried nowhere at all.
1446: They paid so much to be forgotten that, somehow, they are all I can think about now.
1447: They watched me tuck the letter away, then watched my hands the entire time, just in case.
1448: They gave me one small note and instructions so long they became a second, larger note.
1449: They sealed the note in front of me, paid triple, and made me promise not to peek or point.
1450: They gave me the grandest fee of my career for the smallest note I have ever carried.
1451: They asked whether I could read, looked relieved when I said no, and paid me as if unconvinced.
1452: They paid me before handing over the letter, as if the coins were the real message.
1453: They paid triple for speed and triple again for my silence about who sent me.
1454: They pressed a fat purse into my palm to remember the address and forget the sender.
1455: They gave me a note so secret that they paid extra for me to forget it existed.
1456: They pressed the wax seal down themselves, twice, in case the world had somehow missed how important the letter was.
1457: They handed over the note and the coins in complete silence, and I obeyed the silence exactly.
1458: They counted out my fee slowly, adding one more coin each time I promised to hurry.
1459: They gave me the note, the coins, and a warm smile, then asked me to keep only the note.
1460: They bought every last thing on my cart, paid the full price, and asked what I keep for special customers.
1461: I sell trinkets. They took all of them at once and seemed disappointed I had nothing more expensive.
1462: They cleared my whole tray in one breath, then asked if I hid the truly rare things somewhere else.
1463: Never once asked the price. Bought the lot, and looked bored, like my best goods were beneath them.
1464: They emptied my stall without blinking and wanted to know where a person buys something no one else has.
1465: I've sold on this corner for years. Nobody buys everything. They did, and then asked for more.
1466: They pointed at my entire display and said 'all of it,' then frowned that it still wasn't enough.
1467: Paid without counting, took the whole basket, and asked, very seriously, for something no one else owns.
1468: They swept my cart clean, admired themselves in my little mirror, and asked what I keep for the wealthy.
1469: I offered a discount. They waved it away, bought it all, and demanded something far rarer than trinkets.
1470: They bought my full stock so fast I hadn't finished naming a price for the very first thing.
1471: Took everything, tipped me for the effort of packing it, and sniffed that none of it was rare enough.
1472: They bought everything on the cart, then the cloth beneath it, then asked, politely, if the cart itself was for sale.
1473: Empty stall by lunch. Then they leaned close and quietly asked for the one thing nobody else could ever own.
1474: They bought everything, counted it twice to be sure it was truly everything, then asked for more.
1475: No haggling, no counting, just 'all of it' — then a long sigh that I had nothing more special.
1476: They bought all I had, then asked me to point out the one item a person of real taste would envy.
1477: Bought the cart bare in one go, then wanted to know who sells the things too rare for the street.
1478: They emptied my stand and paid me double, but the one thing they truly wanted I did not have.
1479: I named my highest price as a joke. They paid it for everything and then asked for something grander.
